title: Lent, forty days
hook: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving before Easter

segments.voice: Yesterday: the works of mercy, and the king who said I was hungry. Today, the last day of the visit to the Catholic tradition.

One Wednesday in late winter, you might notice something odd on the train. A smudge of gray on someone's forehead. Then another, and another: a nurse, a guy in a suit, a teenager with earbuds. It isn't dirt. It's ash, put there that morning in the shape of a cross, with a few old words: remember that you are dust. It's the first day of a season that runs forty days, and asks people to give something up: Lent.
screen: `A GRAY SMUDGE ON THE TRAIN.` → `REMEMBER THAT YOU ARE DUST.` → `FORTY DAYS.`

segments.voice: The ashes come from Genesis, from God's words to Adam, in the Douay-Rheims translation: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." It sounds grim, but some hear it as freeing: you're not in charge of everything, and the time you have is a gift. Why forty? Because forty keeps turning up in the Bible as a time of testing and preparation: forty days of rain for Noah, forty years for Israel in the wilderness, forty days for Moses on the mountain. And Jesus fasted forty days in the desert before he began to teach. Lent follows him there. It has three practices, all from Jesus' teaching in Matthew six: prayer, fasting and almsgiving, which means giving to the poor. Catholic practice asks for fasting on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and no meat on the Fridays of Lent. People often choose a personal sacrifice too, sweets, social media, a daily coffee, or add something good instead. Count the days from Ash Wednesday to Easter and you get more than forty: in the Western count, Sundays are left out, since each one is kept as a small Easter. Orthodox Christians keep their own Great Lent, starting on a Monday. The English name Lent comes from an old word for spring, the season of lengthening days. Now look back at the week. The Eucharist: real presence. The rosary: one bead at a time. The saints: a cloud of witnesses. Sacred reading: read slowly. The Hail Mary: full of grace. The works of mercy: I was hungry. And Lent: forty days, walking toward Easter.
screen: `FOR DUST THOU ART.` · `FORTY: TESTING AND PREPARING.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, GIVING.` · `LENT — THE LENGTHENING DAYS.` · then, large: `FORTY DAYS.`

segments.voice: Look honestly at your day: what do you reach for without thinking? The phone at red lights, a second dessert, a sharp comment. Choose one to give up just for today, and picture the moment you'll want it, and what you'll do with that gap instead: a breath, a prayer if you pray, a coin for someone.
Lent. From the old English word for spring: forty days of prayer, fasting and giving on the way to Easter. Today's word.
Your line: forty days. That's the whole Catholic week, from real presence to ashes. Tomorrow, a visit to Islam.

howItsDone: Catholics begin Lent with ashes on Ash Wednesday, fast that day and on Good Friday, abstain from meat on Fridays, and take on personal practices of prayer, fasting and almsgiving until Easter.
